prime.problem: Constrained decoding must decide which tokens are legal at every step. Checking all 248,320 tokens against the schema each time is hopeless, so the engine needs a compact way to hold "where am I in the schema?" and look up the answer. A finite state machine is the simplest such memory, and its limits decide which schemas it can serve.
prime.fits: Second card of part 2. Token masking gave you the loop and assumed some oracle supplies the mask. This card is the first real oracle: compile the schema to a regex, the regex to a state machine, and the state machine to a token lookup table.
expect: regex → character FSM → token FSM (the index)
states, transitions, real choices, the accept state
precompute once, O(1) lookup per step
prime.goal: Hand-trace an FSM's state and mask over a short output, explain why its limit on nesting is architectural, and say when its compile cost pays off. Watch four things as you read: grammar expressiveness → state representation → token masking → runtime performance.

attend: What exactly does one FSM state remember, and what does it forget?
How does the character machine become a token machine, and why is that step done before generation instead of during it?
At a state with two allowed tokens, when is that a real choice for the model and when is it just two spellings of the same text?
Why must a machine with finitely many states fail on the Wikipedia link chain, whatever engineering effort goes into it?
What does the precompute buy per step, and what does it cost before the first token?

must: Constraint (regex) → FSM state (how far along the pattern) → allowed transitions → allowed tokens (precomputed per state) → logits mask → sampling: the state is the only thing the engine needs to know to mask

Finite states → no stack or counter → can't track unbounded nesting → a recursive schema needs a separate branch per depth (21·D − 7 states here, infinite without a limit) → recursion needs a CFG/PDA engine

Walk every token from every state once, before generation → each step becomes one table lookup regardless of vocabulary size → but that build is paid up front (Outlines GCT 3.48–12.77 s) → it only pays off when a schema is reused many times

Many token paths spell the same forced text (7 spellings of name, 1,344 paths for 4 outputs) → collapse each forced run to one spelling → the model is asked only at real choices (2 calls instead of 10)
elevated: The token index maps (state, token) → next state → masking is a lookup, not a vocabulary scan → this is why an FSM backend's per-step cost doesn't grow with 248,320 tokens, while its build cost does
Counting keywords (minItems, maxItems, big enums) must be unrolled into states → the index balloons → the paper's 40 s–10 min Outlines timeouts
reference: the toy regex's exact state numbering (0–27) and the 33-row table
the interegular 0.3.3 library used to count states
Outlines' internal index format and API
the break-even arithmetic (≈ 75 reuses on GlaiveAI)

compress.prompt: Draw the pipeline from memory as a chain: regex → character FSM → token index → per-step lookup → mask. Under it, draw one arrow chain for the limit (finite states → … → PDA) and one for the cost (precompute → … → reuse). Aim for three lines total.
checklist: a state records how much valid text has been written, nothing more
the token index stores, per state, the allowed tokens and where each leads
each step is one lookup, whatever the vocabulary size
no stack or counter, so unbounded nesting needs infinite states
the build cost (GCT) is paid per new schema and amortised by reuse
forced runs can be skipped; only real choices need the model

retrieve.q: Explain why an FSM engine can serve a flat schema with a lookup per step but can't serve a recursive one at all, in terms of what a state can remember.
answer: a state is one position in a fixed pattern; there are finitely many
a flat schema has finitely many positions, so every prefix maps to a state
a recursive schema must remember how many objects are open; each depth needs its own states, so unbounded depth needs infinitely many

retrieve.q: Walk through what the engine does between the model producing logits and sampling the next token at state 9 of the toy regex.
answer: look up state 9's row in the precomputed index: John → 16, Paul → 16
mask every other token (24 of the 26 illustrative tokens)
renormalise the model's probabilities over John and Paul, sample one
move to state 16 for the next step

retrieve.q: Your service uses one fixed 10-field schema for millions of calls; another team builds a new schema from each user's CSV header. Which one should use an FSM backend, and what number decides it?
answer: the fixed schema: the build is paid once and spread over every call
the per-request schema pays GCT every time (seconds on Outlines) for no reuse
the deciding number is reuses k vs the build cost: on GlaiveAI the card's arithmetic breaks even near 75 reuses, and never on GitHub-Hard, where Outlines' TPOT is also worse

retrieve.q: The toy regex has 28 character states but the token table only uses 21 of them. Why, and does the model ever lose a valid output because of it?
answer: whole-word tokens like John and age jump over the middle states (10–15, 25)
those states are still reachable by single-character tokens in a real vocabulary, but not in this illustrative one
no output is lost: all 4 strings still reach the accept state

compare.q: FSM vs PDA: what is fundamentally different about the state each one keeps, which design choice gives the FSM its speed and the PDA its reach, when do you pick each, and how does each fail?
answer: FSM: one position in a fixed pattern. PDA: a position plus a stack of what's still open
no stack means everything can be precomputed into a table (fast lookups); the stack lets one small machine handle any depth
pick the FSM for small, flat, reused schemas; the PDA for recursive or deeply nested ones
the FSM fails by state explosion or compile timeouts, and can't express recursion. The PDA fails by per-token stack work that can't all be precomputed, and by letting the model nest without end

compare.q: This card's "2 LLM calls instead of 10" and Guidance's fast-forward both skip forced text. What is the same, and what does an FSM make easier about it?
answer: both notice that only one continuation is legal and append it without asking the model
in a precomputed FSM a forced run is visible at compile time: a chain of states with one way out
an on-the-fly engine must discover it at run time, step by step

predict.q: Four schemas go to an FSM backend: (a) an array of 1 to 1,000 SKUs, (b) an object with 200 optional fields in any order, (c) a comment with replies: [comment], (d) a string matching an email-like regex. Which one first exposes a pure FSM's limit (not just its cost)? Commit before revealing.
predict.answer: (c). It is recursive, so exact support needs unbounded depth, which no finite machine can track: that is a limit of expressiveness. (a) and (b) are finite, so an FSM can represent them, but counting to 1,000 and 200 optional fields in any order both blow up the number of states: that is the cost limit behind the paper's Outlines timeouts. (d) is exactly what regexes are for.

apply.task: Hand-trace the toy regex producing {"name":"Paul","age":30} with the card's 26-token vocabulary, using the fewest tokens ({" name ": " Paul "," age ": 30 }). For each step write the current state, the allowed tokens and how many are masked. Then mark each step as a real choice (different outputs possible) or spelling only (several tokens, same text). Finally, break it: using the card's formula, how many states does a depth-2 link chain need, and what happens at depth 3?
apply.done: You have a 10-row table (state, allowed tokens, masked count, real choice or spelling only) ending in the accept state, plus the state counts for a depth-2 and a depth-3 link chain, all written before you open the check.
apply.hint: Check, only after trying: states 0, 2, 6, 8, 9, 16, 19, 22, 24, 26 → 27 (accept). Allowed counts 2, 4, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 1, so masked 24, 22, 24, 25, 24, 24, 24, 24, 24, 25 of 26. Only state 9 (John/Paul) and state 24 (20/30) are real choices; elsewhere the options spell the same text (at state 6, " and ":; at state 16, " and ","). Depth 2 needs 21 × 2 − 7 = 35 states; a depth-3 input is rejected until you rebuild with 56.
